title: Technology-forcing rules and uncertainty
summary: A technology-forcing rule requires performance that industry may be able to achieve through further development; the agency must explain the prediction.
notes:
Mashaw and Harfst argue that demanding a presently demonstrable factual basis can impede a statutory program designed to induce future innovation. Their account of NHTSA attributes part, but not all, of its retreat from ambitious standards toward recalls to litigation and the burden of defending predictions. They question the assumption that a remand is a modest intervention: staff reassignment, new leadership, and elapsed time can transform or end a project. They also argue that agencies may present artificially linear explanations of a more experimental decision process. These are attributed institutional critiques, rather than holdings.

The contrasting diesel-emissions excerpt explains how review can accommodate uncertainty. EPA had to identify the remaining engineering tasks, answer theoretical objections, and give plausible reasons for believing industry could solve the problems within the available lead time. It did not have to supply every engineering solution. Existing prototypes, recent progress, candidate materials, and manufacturers’ projections supported its prediction about trap-oxidizers. The distinction is between an explained prediction suited to the statute’s forward-looking task and unsupported confidence.
